newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Tropical storms, not army revolt, hit PNG.
newsitem.headline: Tropical storms, not army revolt, hit PNG.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's prime minister on Tuesday said he had survived an attempted coup by his former army chief, but life on the streets of this tropical capital laboured on seemingly unaware of the crisis.
There were no signs of army or police security on Port Moresby's mottled roads as trucks jockeyed with crowded buses during the brief peak hour rush.
Children kicked footballs around rain-soaked fields in the steamy heat and the only rumblings to be heard were from intermittent tropical rainstorms over the city.
Commuters did last-minute shopping before heading home ahead of the daily 10 p.m. to 4.00 a.m. curfew -- which is in place to stem endemic violence.

But inside the nation's parliament, Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan hosted a major news conference with local and international media, declaring his government had just survived one of the nation's worst political crises.
"The government is in absolute control of the situation," Chan said. "The former commander is guilty of gross insubordination and bordering on treason..."

Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok on Monday demanded Chan resign within 48 hours or he would call on the people to oust him. Singirok said he opposed the government's use of foreign mercenaries to end the nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island.
On Monday night, Chan sacked Singirok as commander of the army. The Australian-trained general stepped down quietly on Tuesday and called on his former troops to remain calm.
Singirok could now face criminal charges -- possibly treason.
Why would a career soldier and one-time close ally of Chan try to topple the government one day and meekly step down the next?
Chan believes Singirok was not acting alone.
"The former commander appeared to be, in my assessment, running a number of political agendas," said Chan, who faces a national election in June.
Chan has twice been prime minister of this mountainous South Pacific nation where allegiances are literally bought and sold and political longevity is rare.
Two former leaders, Michael Somare and Paias Wingti, are expected to challenge him in the June election, and corruption is again expected to be a big issue.
And this time, analysts say, Singirok could emerge as a new political figure campaigning on an anti-corruption platform if he manages to escape charges of insubordination.
"If he articulates the notion of eliminating corruption, then that would certainly bring him popular support," said PNG historian Hank Nelson of the Australian National University.
Papua New Guinea normally strictly controls the foreign media it lets into the country, but on Tuesday Chan's government opened the airport gates and welcomed the media with open arms.
"I want to appeal to you distinguished reporters and international media personalities, I appeal to the world press to report this issue responsibly," Chan said.
"Because any speculation or supposition only serves to damage Papua New Guinea's international reputation. This is a situation that we as a developing nation can ill afford."
With an election only three months away, the same could be said of Chan.
